item.title: ‘Indian cricket went through a dark phase’: Sachin Tendulkar's big revelation on captaincy stint
item.description: Cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar has offered an insight into his unsuccessful stints as India's captain, admitting that he did not always have complete control over team selection during his leadership years in the 1990s. Tendulkar, who represented India across formats during an international career spanning 24 years, addressed the subject during an 'Ask Me Anything' session on Reddit on Tuesday. He also named his favourite Indian captains and shared his admiration for South Africa skipper Temba Bavuma. The batting great, who made his international debut on November 15, 1989, and retired on November 16, 2013, described leading India as a tremendous honour. However, he acknowledged that the role came with limitations, particularly when it came to choosing the playing XI. "It was a great honour to lead the team as captain. However, I didn’t always have the freedom to pick my team entirely on my own. The BCCI today is a far more professional organisation than it was in the 1990s. Indian cricket also went through a particularly dark phase during that period," Tendulkar said. Despite his stature as one of the greatest batters in the history of the game, Tendulkar's two separate spells as India's captain in the 1990s did not produce the desired results. Tendulkar names Ganguly and Dhoni as favourite captains When asked about his preferred leaders, the former India captain picked Sourav Ganguly and MS Dhoni, both of whom played significant roles in shaping Indian cricket. "As far as my favourite captains go, Sourav Ganguly and MS Dhoni would definitely be at the top of my list!!," Tendulkar said. Both captains shared memorable World Cup moments with Tendulkar. Under Ganguly, India reached the final of the 2003 ODI World Cup in South Africa, finishing as runners-up. Dhoni, meanwhile, led India to the 2011 ODI World Cup title on home soil, allowing Tendulkar to fulfil his long-standing dream of winning the tournament. Tendulkar praises Temba Bavuma's leadership Tendulkar also had words of appreciation for South Africa captain Temba Bavuma, praising the right-handed batter for leading his team from the front and producing impressive results. "I truly admire Temba Bavuma’s spirit. He has led from the front and delivered some remarkable results for South Africa cricket. South Africa winning an ICC title is great for world cricket!" Bavuma's leadership has been backed by strong performances from the Proteas, including their 2-1 Test series victory over Australia in a three-match contest. The South African captain played a key role in the turnaround, scoring a career-best 179 in the second Test. In the series-deciding third Test at Newlands, off-spinner Simon Harmer delivered a match-winning performance, claiming 10 wickets in the game, including figures of 6/16 in the second innings. Harmer's efforts helped South Africa dismiss Australia for just 111 on the final day and seal the series 2-1. 135528701

item.title: What Kentucky-Tennessee showdown means for SEC football title race
item.description: LEXINGTON — Kentucky football is seeking to seal a spot in the SEC championship game for the first time in program history. To make that a reality, the task — one easier said than done — is simple: just keep winning. UK and coach Will Stein are 5-1 in the SEC this fall. That puts it alongside Georgia for first place in the league entering this week. Every other conference team has at least two league losses. If the Wildcats and Bulldogs win their final three SEC games, they'll square off Dec. 5 in Atlanta. But if either loses? It could get complicated. Kentucky 's three-game stretch to wrap up its conference slate starts Nov. 7 against Tennessee at Neyland Stadium . The Volunteers have won the past five matchups in the series and own an 86-26-9 advantage all-time. Kentucky also has struggled on the road: It's 11-45-6 in Knoxville, Tennessee, versus UT. Next up for Kentucky is Florida on Nov. 14 in Lexington. The Wildcats have won four of the last five against the Gators. Still, it's far from a guaranteed win for Kentucky in a series where it once lost 31 straight games . UK's SEC finale is on the road against the state to the west, Missouri . The Wildcats are up 9-5 in the series , though their 2021 victory was vacated because of NCAA violations. Even so, since Mizzou joined the league ahead of the 2012 season, Kentucky leads 7-5 (including the vacated win). "Not that we shy away from the reality of where we are in terms of our conference rank and our conference record," Stein said Nov. 3, "but if you don't handle your business this week? Then nothing really matters." UGA also is on the road this week, facing Ole Miss . Coach Kirby Smart 's club concludes conference play with Missouri (at home Nov. 14) and South Carolina (on the road Nov. 21). The Rebels won the last meeting: the Sugar Bowl , which doubled as a College Football Playoff quarterfinal in 2025. Georgia , however, has a decisive advantage in the rivalry. The same goes for its records versus Mizzou and South Carolina . There are no gimme games in the conference, of course. Yet it's hard to bet against the Bulldogs, the two-time defending SEC champion (and the team picked to win the league at the outset of the season). item.title: Louisville football OC Brian Brohm finds rhythm in new role as play-caller
item.description: For more than a decade, Brian Brohm exhibited the same kind of patience he's required of his players coming up in the ranks. Louisville football's offensive coordinator waited for his time to be a play-caller, taking a backseat to older brother and head coach Jeff Brohm . Brian had some input and would help put together the game plan, but Jeff had the final say during games. That changed a month ago, when Jeff relinquished play-calling duties to Brian and the Cardinals' offensive staff. "Brian's been with me a long time," Jeff Brohm said on Oct. 12. "He's been with me. He knows the offense. He knows football. He's extremely smart." Brian Brohm was hesitant but prepared. "During the week, I've always been kind of scripting and putting the game plan together, and Jeff would have a couple of inputs here and there," he said. "And his inputs, when you got to game time, he put those in. He's probably going to call those. The ones I'm scripting, I'm probably going to call those. So that's just a little bit more flow of what I was scripting all week, those getting called." The Cardinals' offense has generally looked the same with Brian and Jeff almost always agreeing on what they like and which plays they believe are going to work. Since Brian Brohm took over, the Cardinals are on a three-game winning streak while scoring 43.3 points and totaling 230 passing yards and 269.3 rushing yards per outing. During the team's previous three ACC games, the Cards averaged 34 points, 251.7 passing yards and 184.4 rushing yards, going 1-2 in the process. Louisville's explosive offense will open November by playing at Georgia Tech on Saturday, Nov. 7. The Cards rank second in the country with 20 plays covering 40 or more yards. The Yellow Jackets' defense is one of the worst in the ACC, having allowed 30.8 points and 414.3 total yards per game. They're particularly prone to allowing big plays, too, including 11 that have covered at least 40 yards. Among ACC teams, only Louisville and Stanford have allowed more (12 apiece). "I feel like I've been ready to call the plays for a long time. But at the same point, I think Jeff is one of the top play-callers in the country, and he has been for a long time," Brian Brohm said. "I think that is a difficult decision to step down from calling those plays." One of the biggest lessons he's learned from Jeff is to not second-guess himself, nor be afraid to make the necessary calls, even if it doesn't always work. During Week 9, Louisville tried to fake a field goal against Stanford. The attempt was unsuccessful and resulted in a turnover on downs. But at the same time, Louisville's deep, talented group of skill players can make up for some of the riskier calls. For example, although the trickery didn't work, the Cardinals totaled 52 points and 545 yards of offense, their most against an FBS opponent this season. item.title: Daishi Goto returns to lead Cherry Hill East wrestling program
item.description: Daishi Goto knows there’s toughness in the wrestling room at Cherry Hill High School East. Now, it’s his job to bring it out of his grapplers. Goto was named the head coach of the East wrestling program last month, returning to his alma mater to become the third person to hold the position in the last three years. Goto takes over for Collin Wickramaratna, who went 13-16 in his lone season with the Cougars. The program has had just two winning seasons since 2019. “I’m super excited to be back at my high school as a head coach, it’s going to be a lot of fun,” said Goto, a 2013 East graduate who wrestled and played running back on the football team, once holding the single-season rushing record of 1,587 yards for the Cougars. “When I heard about this opportunity, it just felt like it was meant to be. “People are going to be surprised at the toughness of these Cherry Hill kids. I want to build that mental toughness, too. I want to develop those positive feelings and build the self-confidence in these kids. I know it’s in there.” Cherry Hill East athletic director Mike Beirao believes Goto will be able to develop those traits in the wrestlers. “Daishi is the poster child of putting in the work to be a success,” Beirao said. “He’s such a fiery competitor whose success comes from hard work and doing the extra things to become better. “He has a great vision for the program. It’s going to be about the work and development. That’s how you build a successful program.” A two-time district finalist at East, Goto wrestled at Camden County College where he was a NJCAA All-American under head coach Gary Papa and wrestled alongside national champion Dymere Rappa. Goto would return to CCC as an assistant coach. Goto, who will turn 32 on Thanksgiving, is a black belt in jiu jitsu and a standout grappler for the Abu Dhabi Combat Club. He competed in the 2024 ADCC World Championships and medaled at the 2024 ADCC US Open in Atlantic City. Born in Japan, Goto moved to South Jersey early in his life and was raised in Cherry Hill. He’s the son of two popular professional wrestlers. His father, Seiji, was a star on the All-Japan Pro Wrestling circuit in the early 1980s under his ring name, Tarzan Goto. He would hit the United States pro wrestling circuit in the late 1980s, wrestling some big bouts with Mick Foley (who also went by ring names of Nick Foley and Cactus Jack). The senior Goto died in 2022. Goto’s mom, Despina Montagas, was also a professional wrestler trained by The Fabulous Moolah during the 1980s. She also went by her ring name “Batgirl." Daishi Goto will make his coaching debut when Cherry Hill East opens the 2026-27 season on Dec. 12 with a quad-meet at Cinnaminson. item.title: Joe Mazzulla names one schematic blunder Celtics must fix, it's not about Jayson Tatum
item.description: Joe Mazzulla names one schematic blunder Celtics must fix, it's not about Jayson Tatum originally appeared on The Sporting News . Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Boston Celtics thought they were peachy early in their 2026-27 NBA season. Then, they got slapped with a rough 109-93 loss to the Houston Rockets . Much of their identity on both ends of the floor collapsed. Everyone on Coach Joe Mazzulla's squad scored under 20 points, including Jayson Tatum. The Celtics' head coach admitted they made a schematic blunder after seeing the collapse. It all comes down to how they use Mitchell Robinson. Mazzulla names Celtics' schematic blunder that revolves around Robinson The Celtics were all but ready to face the league-leading Rockets. They were on a five-game winning streak entering this game, then everything fell apart. Jayson Tatum willed Coach Joe Mazzulla's squad to a first-quarter 29-point tie. Afterward, the Celtics just lagged in every aspect of the game. The Celtics did win the rebounding battle, with 38 total boards to the Rockets' 36. However, Coach Mazzulla noted this was the one aspect the Celtics needed to improve. It wasn't that Jayson Tatum and Co. all scored under 20 points; the focus is on fixing their rebounding woes. He further explained the problem on the boards by emphasizing that the Celtics weren't using Mitchell Robinson properly, via Jay King of The Athletic. "I would say for his (Mitchell Robinson) offensive rebounding impact, we have him a little bit further away from the rim, setting screens and playmaking for us on the perimeter as part of our offense. I think that has a little bit to do with it," the Celtics head coach declared. Robinson is averaging only 1.8 offensive rebounds and 4.5 boards in total. That's far from his previous season's average of 8.8 total rebounds and 4.2 offensive rebounds. His ORB% also dropped from a career-high 23.9% to 10.6% over the past few games. The Celtics still have an ORB% of 28.9% as a team, which is 11th in the NBA. However, their defensive rebounding has them sunk to 69%, which is 27th in the league. Sure, Tatum and the Celtics need to score more. However, rebounding remains their biggest woe. Robinson was acquired for this specific reason, but he hasn't been much help so far. Can Coach Mazzulla conjure up schemes to patch all of these problems after getting exposed by the Rockets? item.description: VARDEN — One of the biggest surprises of the 2026 fall sports season has been the electrifying run put together by Western Wayne’s girls volleyball team. The Wildcats struggled mightily during the Lackawanna League campaign, notching just three wins against 11 losses and finishing next to last in the Division I standings. However, coach Darren Thorpe’s squad has caught fire at the perfect moment, posting back-to-back upsets in the District 2 tournament and punching its ticket to the Class AAA finals. Led by battle-tested veterans Olivia Haines, Abbie Washine, Adysen Wargo and Olivia Black, the Wildcats are suddenly the hottest team around. Action gets underway at 5 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 5, at Scranton High School. The Wildcats competed against perennial powerhouses like Abington Heights, North Pocono, Blue Ridge and Dunmore — a brutal schedule that presented one challenge after another. Western Wayne’s season began with four consecutive losses before a 3-2 win over Mountain View on Sept. 10. Four more losses followed until the ‘Cats defeated Scranton 3-1 on Sept. 24. The team would taste victory just once more leading up to the district tournament. But, that’s when things started to gel. item.title: For First Family of Wayne Hills football, honor comes at emotional time
item.description: Everyone in the Olsen family agrees that the real Hall of Famer is Sue. “She should be in the Hall of Fame,” former Wayne Hills coach Chris Olsen says with a laugh, talking about his long-time wife. “She has always been there as a coach’s wife, a player’s wife, going through the good and the bad. She is the matriarch.” Coming up from their home in North Carolina, Chris and Sue will be in Wayne on Nov. 6, as the entire Olsen family – including former Patriots stars Greg, Kevin and Christian – is inducted to the inaugural Wayne Hills Football Hall of Fame Class before the team’s sectional-semifinal game against Somerville. The 2002 football squad, the Patriots' first sectional championship team, will also be honored. “It’s long overdue,” said Tony Giampapa, the committee chairman for the Wayne Hills Hall of Fame. “Now is the perfect time. We knew Coach Olsen would be one of the first people in, but then you realize that every single member of the family deserves it, and that’s what we’re going to do.” The Olsen family’s Wayne Hills football legacy Christian, who died in February 2026 of brain cancer , was a Patriots standout quarterback who took them to three sectional finals. item.description: SUNDERLAND, ENGLAND - SEPTEMBER 16: Enzo Le Fee of Sunderland celebrates scoring his team’s first goal with teammates during the UEFA Europa League 2026/27 League Phase MD1 match between Sunderland AFC and AZ Alkmaar at Stadium of Light on September 16, 2026 in Sunderland, England. Already treading water in the league in a fixture list cramped by the additional demands of the Europa League and the League Cup, the task is hardly going to ease beyond the visit of Chelsea on Sunday and the international break, with eleven more fixtures to fulfil on all fronts before the turn of the year. And yet… The gap to the psychologically dizzy height of 17th spot, the one above the drop zone, is only two points. item.title: FAMU football's Quinn Gray takes trip down memory lane at Alcorn State
item.description: Florida A&M ’s upcoming trip to Lorman, Mississippi, means a little more than just a Southwestern Athletic Conference football game against Alcorn State for Quinn Fordham Gray Sr. Alcorn State was Gray’s first SWAC job and a key step towards him moving up the coaching ladder, as he now leads his alma mater, FAMU . “My opportunity to be on The Reservation was second to none,” Gray reflected. “It gave me my first opportunity to see exactly how the SWAC works, how the game atmospheres were, because you’re talking about somebody that was just really exposed to the MEAC at that time ― was tremendous for me.” After three seasons coaching at a local Tallahassee high school, Lincoln Gray accepted a quarterbacks coach role with the Alcorn State Braves in 2020. It was his second college coaching job, following his stint as an associate head coach and offensive coordinator for the Rattlers. Gray stayed at Alcorn State until 2022. Gray was on staff under Fred McNair, a two-time SWAC championship head coach and five-time East Division winner during his tenure from 2016 to 2023. McNair is now the senior advisor and offensive playcaller for the Southern Jaguars. Gray and McNair recently reunited last Saturday, Oct. 31, as FAMU hosted Southern in Tallahassee for a Week 9 Halloween SWAC game. Southern won 42-14 , and then the coaches shared a moment postgame. “I learned a lot as it relates to being a head coach from him,” Gray said of McNair. “In this profession, it’s a copycat league a lot of times. Some of the things he did, I definitely implemented in what we do here. But at the end of the day, you have to put your own twist and flavor to it.” Following two years at Alcorn State, Gray’s coaching journey continued on the NCAA Division I Football Bowl Subdivision level as the Senior Offensive Analyst at the University of Memphis for the 2022 season. He moved on to a successful three-year stint as head coach at Division II Albany State, culminating in the team’s 2025 Black College Football National Championship. Then Gray returned to FAMU and the SWAC as head coach at the school where he became a Hall of Fame and record-breaking quarterback before playing six years in the National Football League. But he’s forever tied to Alcorn State. The famous secluded, tucked-away campus in rural Lorman fostered a sense of community. To get to campus, drivers must exit the highway and drive down a long, isolated 9-mile stretch of Dr. Walter Washington Parkway (the late former school president), known as “The Stretch,” with the Mississippi River bordering the back of the campus. The nearest gas station is roughly 11-12 miles from campus. “Allowed me to save some money because Amazon wasn’t coming out there,” Gray laughed. “The experience was great, and it gave me an opportunity to understand what SWAC football was all about and gave me a chance to learn under a great coach and coaching staff.” FAMU (2-7, 1-4 in SWAC) at Alcorn State (5-4, 3-2 in SWAC) kicks off at 3 p.m. Easte

item.description: A 2.4-mile swim in the choppy waters of Kailua Bay. Followed by a 112-mile bike ride in intense heat along the Queen Kaʻahumanu Highway. And then what is considered the most physically challenging part – a 26.2-mile run to the finish line in the town of Kona, Hawaii. Estero’s Kayla Pokorny not only conquered this course at the 2026 Ironman World Championship on Oct. 10, she walked away as the events fastest amateur woman after finishing the race in 9 hours, 30 minutes and 57 seconds. An achievement like this – topping her field in an event that attracts athletes from across the globe – didn’t happen overnight. It took two previous, harrowing experiences on this same course. It took months of training – up to 25 hours a week ahead of the October race. It took carving out time during the day while balancing motherhood, like going out on runs during her son’s naptime. “I was just determined to get it right,” Pokorny said. “One day I would get it right, whether it’s the third time or the eighth time.” Pokorny’s third time did prove to be the charm. Her goal was to win the women’s 35-39 age group, which she did, but also ended up the overall non-pro women's champion, besting the next closest competitor by nearly eight minutes. Including the professional athletes competing, Pokorny placed 24th out of 609 women that raced. “I felt so good,” Pokorny said. “It was just one of those days when everything just came easy. It didn’t feel easy, but the pace came easy, and I was just cruising along, and I just kept passing girls and passing girls and passing girls.” Kayla Pokorny discovers her passion Growing up in Minnetonka, Minnesota, Pokorny never could have envisioned becoming an Ironman competitor. After swimming in high school, she felt burnt out and went a while without getting in a pool. Pokorny remembered hearing about a friend from high school competing in an Ironman. “That’s insane,” she said she thought at the time. “I could never do that. But though one of Detroit's most popular and productive players of the 1970s (his 14.3 Baseball Reference WAR from 1970-79 lands him second in the decade among Tigers position players), he's not often mentioned as a franchise legend. Bay Area author Adam Henig explores the Detroit native in his 2026 book, " Baseball's Outcast: The Story of Ron LeFlore ," a biography of one of the most talented Tigers players of all time. Henig lays out LeFlore's life from an impoverished childhood on Detroit's east side, to a prison stint, to a dramatic development as an MLB star, with LeFlore's playing career shortened by drugs and conflicts with managers and team executives. Henig's book also picks up where LeFlore's memoir left off, mapping out the star's life after baseball and his legacy in Tigers history. In his discussions with LeFlore's family, former teammates and former Free Press writers, Henig also reveals several details about LeFlore's career in baseball and what eventually led to the game turning away from him. The Free Press spoke to Henig about his writing process and thoughts about LeFlore, with the following interview edited for length and clarity. item.title: Today in Boston Celtics history: Boston sees the Grateful Dead in concert; Shaw, Hunter debut
item.description: Today in Boston Celtics history, several members of the storied franchise went to see a Grateful Dead in concert in Worcester, Massachusetts in 1985. Not all of the Celtics went, but after recent arrival Bill Walton had managed to pique the interest of a few of his teammates, a significant portion of the team decided to attend the concert. A few days ahead of the planned concert, Hall of Fame teammates Larry Bird and Kevin McHale had noticed some hippie-ish looking people wearing funky clothes arriving in town and made the connection it must have something to do with their hippie-ish teammate. Walton had himself previously met the band after sticking out like a sore thumb as a 7-footer at one of their concerts, catching the eye of drummer Mickey Hart, who called him on stage after learning who he was. Teammates Kevin McHale and Larry Bird pulled him aside after practice one day close to the concert. "They said, 'What’s going on?'" Walton explained to Jeff Zillgitt. "I told them, 'Getting ready to practice'". "Nah, something’s going on here. All kinds of new people in town. They’ve got long hair and they’re wearing these crazy shirts that you always wear and everything smells different." “I have no idea what you guys are talking about.” “Are the Grateful Dead coming to town?” “Yes.” “Are you going?” “Yes, I am.” “Can we come, too?” “I believe we can make this happen.” Recent Virginia graduate Rick Carlisle had seen the Dead while at that school and joined them as well. "I went to a lot of shows with Bill and ended up getting to know the guys in the band and some of their stage crew," he related to Zillgitt. One player who didn't? Danny Ainge. Contrary to rumors, his wife did not stop him from going – he just didn't like the music. "I could have gone if I wanted to. I just didn’t want to go," Ainge explained. The teammates who did go met up at Bird's house to take a limousine to the concert, and the following day, the Dead attended a Celtics practice, Bird even challenging drummer Mickey Hart to some 1-on-1. "It was humiliating, to say the least,” Hart said. "I couldn’t even get a shot off. He started checking me really hard, and I said, ‘Hey Larry, I’ve got to play (drums) tonight.’" That night, they went back again to a second show in Worcester, and Walton had the band sing him "Happy Birthday" to close out the exchange program of sorts with festivities. "It was an incredible blend of two cultures that stand for so much of the same things: working together to make a better tomorrow with hope, optimism, peace, and love – important values," said Walton.
